claims.text: Persistence of a coherent protective oxide scale above 900 °C is governed by the local availability of Al and/or Cr.
Al can form a protective Al2O3 layer with high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Al2O3 or Cr2O3 scales are sufficiently adherent to resist cracking and spallation.
Low availability of Al and Cr favors mixed oxides or spinels that are prone to spallation.
The comparison will include single-phase and multiphase CrFeCoNiX solid solutions with comparable grain sizes and thermomechanical histories.
X content and the Al:Cr ratio will be varied while process history and other elemental concentrations are held constant.
The alloys will be exposed at 900 °C or above for at least 100 hours in air or 20% O2/80% N2.
Al and Cr redistribute by diffusion to form dense, continuous scales at the alloy/scale interface.
Local composition and phase distribution moderate oxide-scale formation.
A coherent α-Al2O3 or Cr2O3 layer forms and persists when interfacial Al or Cr remains above a critical concentration threshold.
Below the proposed Al or Cr threshold, Mn or Fe forms non-protective spinels or mixed oxides with poor adhesion.
Alloys with sufficiently high Al:Cr content will show slow parabolic rather than near-linear oxidation kinetics.
Alloys with sufficiently high Al:Cr content will exhibit minimal scale spallation.
Mn-rich or Al/Cr-deficient variants will develop thicker, porous scales that crack or peel more readily.
The control is a single-phase CrFeCoNiMn alloy without deliberate Al addition, exposed under the same conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies at temperatures of at least 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments and in both single-phase and multiphase CrFeCoNiX alloys.
The critical Al and Cr levels are not known precisely and may depend on grain boundaries, phase segregation, and minor additions.
Stable scales on low-Al/Cr alloys, or scale failure on high-Al/Cr alloys, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The principal conditions specify isothermal exposure, whereas the falsification experiment specifies cyclic oxidation and the baseline refers to the same cycle time. Thermal cycling introduces adhesion stresses and is not the same controlled exposure mode as an isothermal test.

The intervention proposes varying X and the Al:Cr ratio while holding other elemental concentrations constant, whereas the experiment describes increasing Al or Cr while keeping overall stoichiometry otherwise constant. Because atomic fractions must sum to 100%, the compensating composition changes are not defined.
